title: Streaming decode cluster SKU interaction notes
content:
Summary:
This is a working note capturing experiments where we compare streaming decode behavior across A100/H100/L40S cloud SKUs and multiple driver/CUDA combos. Focus is on end-to-end 95/99/99.9 latency for streaming (prefill + decode split), CPU-GPU handoff jitter, and cross-VM PCIe/NUMA interactions when the serving cluster is congested. These are not final conclusions — rough observations and action items.

Motivation / why this matters:
- Most production traffic for conversational features uses streaming decode (prefill, then token-by-token decode).
- Small increases in decode tail latency cascade into perceived UI slowness; billing/throughput is dominated by token cost but SLA is latency at the user-facing level.
- Prior SKU benchmarks focus on large-batch throughput; we need a focused investigation on low-batch streaming behavior across driver/runtime versions and cluster-level interference.

High-level experiment design:
- Workloads: (1) Short-context chat (prefill 32 tokens, decode 128 tokens, step-size=1 streaming), (2) Long-context batch (prefill 2048, decode 512), (3) Prefix-heavy reuse (many repeated prefixes to exercise KV cache).
- Models: web-llm-13b and web-llm-70b (fp16 + q4 variants where available).
- SKUs: cloud A100-40GB (n1), H100-80GB (n2), L40S-48GB (n3) — use region equivalents to capture driver packaging differences.
- Drivers/CUDA: Nvidia driver 535.x + CUDA 12.1, 525.x + CUDA 11.8, 535.x + CUDA 12.2 (where available).
- Measurement points: prefill time, first-token latency, steady-state per-token p50/p95/p99/p99.9, CPU ns/interrupts during decode, PCIe bandwidth spikes, kernel launch rate, device-side SM utilization traces.
- Topology control: pin processes to cores, disable hyperthreading for tests, isolate NIC interrupts on dedicated cores.

Test harness (commands & notes):
- Launch a continuous stream runner that records timestamps for: request-send, prefill-complete, first-token-emitted, each token arrival.
- Use perf_event for CPU-side sampling and nvprof / Nsight Systems for GPU traces (wall clock synchronized via NTP).
- Use repeated runs (10x) per combo, clear caches/evict KV between runs when needed.

Key observations (raw):
1) A100 (driver 525/CUDA11.8) had consistent first-token latency for short-context but per-token jitter increased when host-side CPU was under 30% load from other agents. We saw token arrival jitter spikes aligning with periodic host-side GC/housekeeping threads in the runtime.

2) H100 with driver 535 + CUDA12.1 showed better steady-state per-token throughput under high batch-packing, but when running streaming (step=1) the driver introduced 1–3ms kernel launch jitter at unpredictable intervals. These correlated with nvlink link retraining events in the host dmesg under heavy prefill.

3) L40S generally had lower variance in prefill but exhibited larger p99 decode latency for long-context (>=2048) due to KV eviction patterns and host-device transfer behavior; DMA queued spikes were visible.

4) Across all SKUs, switching driver minor versions (525 -> 535) changed tail behavior more than expected. The same CUDA minor upgrade reduced p95 in some SKUs but increased p99. Suggests scheduler/kernel changes that affect tail more than median.

5) PCIe root complex locality: colocating other NVMe IO-heavy processes on same host produced periodic stalls that showed up as token lulls of 2–10ms. Effect strongest on A100 hosts where NVMe-to-GPU DMA path shares root complex.

6) Prefill vs decode split matters: when prefill pinned the GPU for a long contiguous period then decode started, the kernel launch path for tiny decoding kernels saw an initially low latency then tail spikes as host-side queues rebounded. In H100 we observed NV driver throttling heuristics that appear to favor sustained big kernels over many tiny ones (likely power scheduling/SM allocation heuristics).

Anomalies / interesting traces:
- In one H100 run (535/CUDA12.1), kernel launch timestamps had micro-bursts: groups of 6–8 tokens emitted within 4ms, then a pause of ~30ms, repeating. NVLink counters showed periodic queue flushes. Hypothesis: driver is coalescing small launches to optimize throughput, but coalescing interacts badly with streaming SLOs.
- On L40S hosts, we had an incident where p99 decode jumped 40% after a kernel driver patch - dmesg shows "GPU thermal governor invoked" even though host temps were normal; suspect a firmware/driver mismatch.

Quick quantitative summary (median across runs, approximate):
- Short chat (prefill32/decode128): A100(525): first-token 45ms p95 120ms p99 220ms; H100(535): first-token 40ms p95 95ms p99 280ms; L40S(535): first-token 55ms p95 140ms p99 300ms.
- Long-context (prefill2k/decode512): A100: p95 360ms p99 820ms; H100: p95 320ms p99 1200ms (rare stalls); L40S: p95 380ms p99 950ms.
- Prefix-heavy (cache hit): per-token p95 lowered ~30–40% on H100 relative to cold, A100 lowered ~15–25%. L40S had mixed results due to DMA spikes.

Hypotheses and root cause candidates:
- Driver-level coalescing/scheduling heuristics are optimized for high-throughput kernels and can add latency for tiny streaming kernels.
- PCIe/NVMe shared root complex congestion translates to DMA stalls and token gaps — even when GPU SMs are idle.
- Firmware/driver mismatches on L40S cause unexpected thermal governors or power-state transitions for certain micro-bursts.
- Host-side interrupt/CPU scheduling (ksoftirqd, rt throttling) can align with token emission intervals creating periodic tails.

Recommended short-term mitigations to test quickly:
- Force synchronous kernel launches for streaming decode (disable any coalescing flags if present) and measure tail. Add flag-based runtime toggle to quickly A/B.
- CPU isolation for runtime process: pin interrupt affinity away from runtime cores; test disabling C-states and/or increasing CPU governor to performance.
- Migrate NVMe IO heavy workloads off hosts that serve low-latency streaming. For Dedicated pools provide a "low-noise" NVMe assignment.
- Try driver rollback/forward matrix for problem SKUs: run 525.85, 535.54, 536.x where available and log nv-host logs (nv-host-analytics).

Longer-term / infra changes to consider:
- Introduce scheduled micro-batching for streaming where client latency budget allows: group 2–4 tokens when latency impact acceptable to reduce kernel launch frequency.
- Expose driver-scheduler knobs in Dedicated configuration (experimental) and A/B test at 1% traffic.
- For Private deployments, include a pre-flight SKU-driver compatibility check that tests the streaming microbench and rejects known bad combos.

Outstanding experiments (next runs):
- Explicitly reproduce H100 kernel coalescing: run synthetic micro-kernel loop with step=1 but disable other traffic; record kernel dispatch patterns from Nsight.
- Run a cross-region test maintaining identical instance types but different cloud builds to isolate vendor packaging differences (we saw region anomalies once).
- Re-run L40S with firmware vX.Y that vendor shipped last quarter and the new 536 driver to see if thermal governor artifact persists.
- Trace user-space to kernel boundary with eBPF to capture ksoftirqd and timer wake patterns aligning with token pauses.

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Add a small instrumentation patch to the runtime that marks kernel launch IDs in logs so we can correlate GPU-side kernel names with token ids.
- Add a small telemetry metric: streaming-token-lull-count (>=10ms gaps) at p50/p95/p99, exposed in Console for quick triage.
- File a ticket for infra to try dedicated NVMe-less hosts for a low-noise pool.

References and artifacts from runs (raw):
- Nsight system traces (s3://redwood-infra-bench/streaming-traces/2025-02-03-h100-535-c12-1.tgz)
- perf + eBPF traces (s3://redwood-infra-bench/streaming-traces/2025-02-04-a100-525-perf.tgz)
- Short notebook with plots (linked in PR GH-PR above)

Concluding quick take:
Streaming decode tail behavior is sensitive to driver/firmware and to host-level IO/interrupt noise in non-obvious ways. H100 gives the best median for steady decode but is susceptible to driver coalescing artifacts that blow up p99 in some runs. L40S can be very competitive but watch firmware/driver pairings and DMA path behavior. We should instrument more deeply (kernel launch id correlation, eBPF wake traces) and add a small dedicated low-noise pool for customer-facing streaming SLOs.

Open questions for the group:
- Are there known driver knobs (from vendor notes) to force serial kernel dispatch for tiny kernels?
- Can infra provide a 2-node dedicated NVMe-free pool next week for a quick A/B test?
- Any objections to landing the runtime toggle to disable kernel coalescing (feature flag behind config)?

-- Priya
